I found three new dated forecasts from 2026. All three are about how much computing power AI will use, so you may decide they're business forecasts and drop them. I found no new dated prediction about what AI will be able to do that I could quote from a page I opened.

**Where the three come from**
- **His MIT Technology Review essay (8 April 2026), his own words.** He wrote that the world was "looking at something like another 1,000x in effective compute by the end of 2028." In the next paragraph he said this would drive "the transition from chatbots to nearly human-level agents." That second sentence names no date itself; it gets one only from the paragraph before.
- **The Builders podcast with Walter Isaacson, from a transcript.** He said compute applied to models would grow "another 100 to 1,000x" in "the next 3 years." The 12 October 2026 taping date comes only from a search snippet of a podcast listing I didn't open. This seems to be the same session as your existing 2026-10-12 materials file, but that part of the transcript didn't load for me.
- **His Build 2026 keynote (2 June), official transcript.** He said "three more orders of magnitude of compute" would come "in the next few years." That timing is too vague to count, so I've left it in the search log only.

**What's already recorded or set aside**
- **The February "12 to 18 months" white-collar claim** turned up in many news reports. You already have it.
- **The "AI companion for everyone in five years" quote** is widely reported for January 2026, but I couldn't confirm it:
  - The Windows Central page loaded without its article text, and the X post and podscripts pages wouldn't open, so I haven't quoted it.
  - When it was said is unclear. IBTimes ties it to Davos on 20 January, but other coverage traces it to an X video clip posted around 15–16 January, before Davos. The original recording may be older.
- **A forum post** listing predictions for 2026, 2030 and the early 2030s appears to be an AI-written rewrite of the April essay. Those lines aren't in the essay, so I ignored it.
